text: You now know the main distributions. This lesson shows how to draw random data from them with numpy, and why that skill is so valuable. Simulation lets you build fake datasets to test code, answer probability questions you can't solve by hand — the Monte Carlo method — and check that your intuition about a formula is right. It underpins everything in the sampling chapter that follows.

Modern numpy uses a generator object — create it with a seed, and every run gives the same numbers, reproducible for teammates and your future self. default_rng of 2024, then integers from 1 to 7, excluding the upper bound, simulates a six-sided die, and gives the exact same five rolls every time you seed it the same way. Different numpy versions can produce different streams from the same seed, so record your version if exact repeatability matters.

The generator has a method for each family: binomial, poisson, normal, exponential, lognormal, uniform. Building a fake customer table of 10,000 rows with poisson visits, lognormal order values, binomial returns, and normal delivery times, then describing it: the Poisson mean comes out close to 3, the return rate close to 0.30, delivery time close to a mean of 40 and spread of 5.

Notice the huge maximum order value of 668 — the log-normal's long tail at work. A fake table like this is great for practicing pandas or testing a pipeline before real data arrives. Monte Carlo means estimating a probability by repeating a random experiment many times and counting — what's the chance two dice sum to 10 or more? The exact answer is 6 over 36, about 0.1667, and 100,000 simulated rolls land at 0.1653.

Monte Carlo really pays off when no simple formula exists. Suppose a shop processes 50 orders a day, order values are log-normal, and 30 percent are returned. Simulating 20,000 days at once, vectorized: average kept revenue is about 1,389, a bad day at the 5th percentile is about 1,073, and roughly 1.8 percent of days fall below 1,000.

Each row is one simulated day, and this vectorized style is far faster than a Python loop. The answer is only as good as your assumptions — if returns really cluster together, this model understates the true risk.

Simulation error shrinks as you draw more, but slowly. Estimating P of X equals 3 for a binomial with n equals 10, p equals 0.3, whose exact value is 0.2668: with 10 draws you get 0.3, way off. With 100 draws, 0.28. With 1,000, 0.277. With 100,000, 0.2658 — within about 0.001 of the true answer.

Because the error shrinks roughly with the square root of the number of draws, quadrupling the draws only halves the noise. To recap: seed a default_rng, draw from the distribution that matches your story, and build fake data or run Monte Carlo experiments with vectorized numpy. Simulation gives approximate answers with a controllable error, and it's only as trustworthy as the assumptions inside it.
